jurisdiction.name: Mauritius
jurisdiction.overview: Nationally published records appear separately from applicable EU-level records. The landscape, historical relationships and legal applicability remain under document-level review.

narrative.summary: Mauritius governs AI through its 2026 national strategy, AI for Mauritius (AIM), which replaces the 2018 strategy, and the non-binding FAIR Guidelines, both led by the ICT ministry's AI Unit. Government services must carry out an algorithmic impact assessment before deploying AI under the Digital Service Framework, and the Data Protection Act 2017 regulates automated decisions. Binding AI rules are sector-specific: the financial regulator's 2021 rules licensing robotic and AI-enabled advisory services, its 2025 guidance on responsible AI in financial services, and the Higher Education (Use of Artificial Intelligence) Regulations 2026. There is no general AI law; a National AI Council is planned.
lead_institutions: Ministry of Information Technology, Communication and Innovation (Artificial Intelligence Unit)
narrative.review_notes: This review was carried out on 12 October 2026 from documents read in full on official sites. Mauritius is a party to the Council of Europe's data protection convention (Convention 108) since 2016, but no Mauritian accession record could be read on an official site, so the convention is not yet linked. A revised data protection law, the National AI Council and a national data strategy are tracked as leads.

instruments.english_title: AI for Mauritius (AIM): National Artificial Intelligence Strategy - A National Vision for Responsible AI and Regional Leadership

instruments.current_status: Launched on 9 April 2026 at the J & J Auditorium, Phoenix (MITCI news item of 10 April 2026: 'officially launched yesterday'), together with the FAIR Guidelines. Published by the AI Unit as a flipbook with PDF download on aim.govmu.org and also listed under Strategies on mitci.govmu.org. The Prime Minister's foreword is dated 13 February 2026. Replaces the archived Mauritius Artificial Intelligence Strategy of November 2018 (MITCI now files the 2018 document as archived). Previously recorded under the site-page title 'AI Strategy - Artificial Intelligence Unit'.
instruments.summary: Mauritius' National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, built on the Digital Transformation Blueprint 2025-2029 and the Government Programme 2025-2029, with forewords by the President and the Prime Minister (the latter dated 13 February 2026). It sets five strategic pillars (including innovation and research, skills and education) and an AI4AI awareness and literacy programme, and proposes an AI governance framework that, rather than an immediate single AI Act, empowers sector regulators (FSC, HEC, Bank of Mauritius, ICTA, Data Protection Commissioner) to issue guidelines and codes, supported by regulatory sandboxes and a National AI Council (to be constituted) as central coordinating authority. It assigns lead authorities for cybersecurity (CERT-MU/NCC), data protection (DPIA templates, audits), AI procurement guidelines and model/dataset registers (MITCI/National AI Council) and skills.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Current national AI strategy; anchors the FAIR Guidelines, the AI implementation playbook and the proposed sector-regulator governance model.

instruments.official_title: FAIR Guidelines for the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence
instruments.english_title: FAIR Guidelines for the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence
instruments.issuing_authority: Ministry of Information Technology, Communication and Innovation (AI Unit)
instruments.current_status: Launched on 9 April 2026 together with the National AI Strategy (MITCI news item of 10 April 2026). The 38-page PDF carries no date of its own. The guidelines describe themselves as non-binding. Also published on mitci.govmu.org (Strategies and Policies pages, file FINAL-GUIDELINES-15AVRIL.pdf).
instruments.summary: Non-binding national guidelines, grounded in Fairness, Accountability, Inclusiveness and Integrity, and Responsibility, for public institutions, private organisations and technopreneurs developing or using AI in Mauritius. They set a shared-governance model of roles, AI lifecycle controls from design to decommissioning, a risk-based model with low, medium, high and unacceptable risk tiers and escalation safeguards, and chapters on data protection alignment, transparency and human oversight, auditability and record-keeping, procurement and vendor governance, and generative, foundation and agentic AI. A final chapter sets the trajectory from guidelines to policy and legislation, indicating which elements may later become binding.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: National AI ethics and risk framework; the reference for public-sector and private AI use pending any legislation.

instruments.summary: Government's 2025-2029 digital transformation roadmap, aligned with the Government Programme 2025-2029, built on four pillars and a set of enablers. Its Enabler 5 'Data Protection and Artificial Intelligence' commits to a National Data Strategy (2025-2030) that prepares for safe, trustworthy and ethical AI adoption, to formulating a National AI Strategy, and to AI uses in government (automation, virtual assistants, predictive analytics); it also refers to an AI Office and AI regulatory frameworks.

instruments.summary: Mandatory policy framework for public-sector digital services, setting architecture principles, core policy mandates, design standards and compliance mechanisms for all ministries. Its policy 4.14 'Responsible AI and Emerging Technologies' requires an Algorithmic Impact Assessment before any government AI system is deployed, requires AI-driven decisions affecting rights or entitlements to be explainable, auditable and contestable, bars ministries from deploying unverified 'black box' algorithms without oversight, and makes pilots of new technologies subject to MITCI approval; ethical use of algorithms and AI must follow MITCI guidance.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Binding-in-scope public-sector rule requiring algorithmic impact assessments for government AI.

instruments.current_status: Act 20 of 2017, assented 22 December 2017, Government Gazette No. 120 of 23 December 2017; proclaimed in force from 15 January 2018 (Proclamation No. 3 of 2018). The consolidated text on the DPO site notes an amendment by Act No. 1 of 2020. The Digital Service Framework (2026) refers to a forthcoming revised Data Protection Act.
instruments.summary: Mauritius' GDPR-aligned data protection law establishing the Data Protection Office and Commissioner and governing all processing of personal data, including for AI training and use. Section 38 gives data subjects the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal or similarly significant effects, with exceptions and safeguards (human intervention, expressing a view, contesting the decision); controllers must disclose the existence and logic of automated decision-making, and section 34 requires data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Binding legal basis for AI data processing and automated decision-making; cited by the FAIR Guidelines, the FSC AI guidance and the National AI Strategy.

instruments.current_status: Issued by the Data Protection Office on 17 April 2020 (date on cover); still listed on the DPO 'Guidelines Data Protection Act 2017' page. Pandemic-specific; no later revision found.
instruments.summary: Guidance from the Data Protection Office on applying the Data Protection Act 2017 to health data and AI solutions used against COVID-19. It sets out lawful bases under sections 28 and 29, and for AI solutions recommends responsible use in line with data protection principles, including pseudonymisation in algorithms, data minimisation and transparency of automated processing to individuals.

instruments.official_title: Financial Services (Robotic and Artificial Intelligence Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021
instruments.english_title: Financial Services (Robotic and Artificial Intelligence Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021
instruments.current_status: Government Notice No. 128 of 2021 (Government Notices 2021, pp. 1729-1737). Made by the Financial Services Commission on 12 June 2021 and in operation from 12 June 2021; publication_date is the making date because the gazette issue date is not shown on the reproduced text.
instruments.summary: FSC Rules made under section 93 of the Financial Services Act (Government Notice No. 128 of 2021) creating a Robotic and Artificial Intelligence Enabled Advisory Services licence, without which no person may provide digital, personalised advisory services through computer programs or AI-enabled algorithms with limited human intervention. Licensees must keep a Mauritian office and bank account, governance and cyber-risk controls, minimum capital of MUR 600,000 and indemnity insurance, and must have oversight of their algorithms (monitoring that they perform as intended, periodic and random testing, competent staff reviewing methodologies) and keep records of all algorithms and software used. The Rules define 'artificial intelligence', a definition later reused by the Higher Education (Use of AI) Regulations 2026.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Binding sectoral licensing regime for AI-driven (robo-)advisory services.

instruments.english_title: Guidance Notes on the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Financial Services (Fintech Series Guidance Notes 4)
instruments.current_status: Dated September 2025; FSC communiqué of 19 September 2025 (https://www.fscmauritius.org/media/206405/communique-guidance-notes-on-the-responsible-use-of-ai-in-financial-services.pdf) states the Guidance Notes were issued and are effective from 19 September 2025 and urges licensees to incorporate them.
instruments.summary: FSC guidance for insurance, wealth-management and non-bank financial licensees on the responsible and ethical use of AI, setting nine key non-binding principles (appendix) and stressing that AI use should support fair customer outcomes within existing governance, risk-management and internal-control frameworks. It reminds licensees that section 38 of the Data Protection Act 2017 requires informing data subjects of automated decision-making, explaining its logic and allowing human intervention and contestation, and that a DPIA is required before implementing high-risk AI systems.

instruments.summary: Guidelines from the higher education regulator, developed with Commonwealth of Learning support, on adopting AI across higher education institutions. They cover governance, teaching, learning, assessment and research, and ethics, addressing academic integrity, disclosure of AI-generated content, data protection, cybersecurity and intellectual property, for staff, researchers, administrators and students.

instruments.official_title: Higher Education (Use of Artificial Intelligence) Regulations 2026
instruments.english_title: Higher Education (Use of Artificial Intelligence) Regulations 2026
instruments.issuing_authority: Minister of Tertiary Education, Science and Research (under section 51 of the Higher Education Act 2017)
instruments.current_status: GN No. 39 of 2026, Government Gazette of Mauritius No. 25 of 11 April 2026. Made by the Minister on 3 April 2026; regulation 6 states they come into operation on 31 March 2026 (before the making date, as printed). Text read from the HEC's reproduction annexed to its AI guidelines PDF; the gazette issue itself was not read.
instruments.summary: Regulations under the Higher Education Act 2017 (GN No. 39 of 2026) applying to the use of AI in the higher education sector. They empower the Higher Education Commission to issue AI guidelines, directives and standards, prohibit AI uses leading to bias, breaches of academic integrity or plagiarism or of data protection, IP or cybersecurity law, and require corrective measures. Every higher education institution must adopt and update an institutional AI policy, integrate AI into curricula, require disclosure and acknowledgement of AI-generated content in coursework and research, monitor AI use, and put safeguards in place to protect human rights and dignity.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Binding AI-specific sectoral regulation for higher education.
